This is a great game and I would recommend everyone plays it. Despite not being a AAA title, it has a wonderful aesthetic, runs very smoothly, and has very few bugs and exploits that I can see, after having played through the game twice. There's a metroid-vania style of finding new keys (ciphers) and seeing what crap you can unlock, and while the game is somewhat linear in design, it's more in the same way that Dark Souls is. You have to beat 3 bosses to unlock the second part of the game. Then you have to beat 3 bosses to unlock the end of the game. Then you beat the end of the game. Very Bells of Awakening, Lord Souls, Gwyn feel here.

Some pros:
- Worlds are very interconnected and seem to make a ton of sense. You only have 3 worlds to explore, but they are varied and are intertwined with each other so you'll pop out somewhere and say "oh... those were doors the whole time?!"
- The worlds themselves are really good and each have their own theme. Very interesting places with lots of diversity despite only being 3 worlds.
- There's lots of crap to find. Some of it very useful, some of it less useful, but it always feel good to walk up to a chest and know you can open it because you have all the necessary collectibles. Again, very Metroid-vania.
- Bosses are cool and dynamic. A little on the easy side, but cool all the same. There's minibosses as well if you can find them, and they offer cool rewards.

Some Cons:
- Gun balance is way off. Single shot high damage weapons are king and everything else is... not. You also get 5 legendary assault rifles, all of which are not as good as a green sniper rifle, even upgraded all the way.
- Enemies. There's like 10 enemies in the game, and reskins of those. Some of them are bosses you fought earlier, some of them are basic enemies. Basic enemies hit harder than most every boss. In fact, I would say the bosses are down right easy compared to some of the areas.
- Pop-in. Enemies can summon out of nowhere. This is nonsense and makes the game impossible to plan around unless you've done an area over and over and over again until you know exaclty when and where they will pop up. Whether it's teleporting or crawling out of the ground, like I said, these enemies hit harder than the bosses and will gank you at every turn.

Suggestions for Devs:
- Add a checklist type thing. Let me hover over a world and see how many Cerium Decrees, Protheium Edicts, etc. I've collected. Let me see how many locked chests I have to open. I've been through the game fully twice and there's stuff I haven't found because I cannot figure out if it's even there. It's a collectathon (especially for the Easter Egg type stuff at the end game), there should be some form of check list.
- Balance your weapons. **MINOR SPOILERS IN SECTION**. Grenade Launchers and Sniper rifles are too good. They have essentially unlimited ammo, and most things die in one hit. Acid type weapons suck really hard, while pure physical weapons can beat nearly every enemy in the game. One boss is nearly impossible without a physical weapon.

Do I think it's worth $50? To me, I got at least that much enjoyment out of it. And will likely get more. If you can wait for another soulslike, you can wait for this game to go on sale. HOWEVER for a first attempt at a 3rd person shooter soulslike, this game is very well done! It's graphically attractive, light on bugs, and can easily take up a whole weekend.

I was honestly surprised when only a few games rose to challenge Dark Souls for dominance of whatever that kick-you-in-the-ass-but-you-love-it genre is called. I shouldn’t be, because the formula that launched the Souls games into the ionosphere is an incredibly complex one and extremely tricky to replicate. Some of those games that did rise in its wake, such as Immortal: Unchained, managed to hit a tantalizing number of the high points, including clever level design and interesting gearing. But there are always soft spots in the design, and Immortal’s soft spots are squishy enough to fall right through if you’re not willing to fight through some tedium and frustration.

I can give you a loose rundown of the plot to Immortal: Unchained, but even as far in as I am much of it is obscured by piecemeal plot snippets. The Core exists as the de facto center of the universe, a vast technological morass controlled by the Monolith, a nigh-incomprehensible super computer. Originally the product of the industrious Primes, it fell into irrelevance as the Prime empire crumbled and galactic society was ravaged by legions of the cyber-undead. You are an Immortal, a chosen of the Primes, broken free from eternal imprisonment to stop this scourging wave and save the universe from total oblivion. Along the way you’ll meet a handful of unstable folks riding out the galactic apocalypse and find plenty of snippets of deeper lore, which I’m having trouble recalling at the moment.

Look, I know everyone wants to do the measured, environmental storytelling of Dark Souls but whatever it is that’s going on here is too offbeat and dense for that. The setting feels heavily 40K inspired but with more mystical elements, and the way information is parsed out won’t really help you fill in the gaps here. You’re fighting space undead for a giant slab of stone, that much is certain, but the nature of the Monolith and its caretaker, or the relevance of the three worlds you’ll travel to, or the details of the many fallen empires you’ll dig through get explored in a thin, patchy way that makes the story too difficult to connect with.

What isn’t difficult to connect with is the combat, which is essentially a third-person shooter take on Dark Souls. Your Immortal can carry a sidearm and a primary (eventually unlocking two additional primary slots), which run the gamut from pistols and revolvers to assault rifles and grenade launchers. They’re all appropriately space-agey with neon tubes and strange protrusions, and come with special attacks like freezing blasts and fire barrages triggered off your energy bar. The weapons themselves have a wall of stats including damage scaling, element type, stagger effect, and reload speed. You get a melee weapon as well but the combat is a bit too stiff and bursty to really rely on it. Just as early Souls games were melee affairs with ranged options, Immortal: Unchained is very much a shooter with melee diversions.

You’ll use these weapons to pop the heads and capacitors of all sorts of glowing undead jackasses, from basic shambling skeletons to massive shielded sentinels. They all have their patterns and predictable moves, though some can be far more obnoxious than others. Midway through the game you’ll start facing off against snipers that teleport and track you with deadly accuracy, and raiders with dual tommy guns that can melt you in an instant. Provided you have a decent weapon and keep it upgraded you won’t run into too many roadblocks, though the boss of the forest planet proved to be a tooth-grinding hassle that I feared was impossible for me. With a wide-area ranged attack he could chain and a near instant-kill close-range spin, he made life for my sniper build hell until I was able to land a few lucky shots on his weak point.

That’s really the core of the game, sniping or spraying weak points as you methodically work through the levels. Locational damage is important but none so important as those glowing weak spots, as bigger enemies can have absurd, almost bossish health pool to whittle down. That might be because weapon damage can go entirely off the rails with the right finds, upgrades, and skills, but it can also be woefully weak if you get dealt a bad hand. I had to restart the game once because the first class I picked could only really use ineffectual rifles and pistols. Starting over as a sniper made a huge difference to my enjoyment, but it still took an inordinate amount of time to learn the real flow of this game.

Once place I can unequivocally praise Immortal: Unchained is in the level design. Everything you loved about Dark Souls is here, from twisting paths to hidden chests to secret shortcuts and more. Some of the ways the levels connect back to the save monoliths over and over are simply brilliant, and add a lot to the exploration. The art doesn’t quite hold up as well, with most environments looking a bit bland and samey, a sensation you will experience plenty right from the start in the many ice-blue cubist walls of your prison. The rest of the presentation is solid, though, with competent voice acting, decent sound effects, and easily-parsed menus.

If I sound decidedly middle-of-the-road on this one, it’s because I want to temper expectations. Dark Souls has some cavernous shoes to fill, and Immortal: Unchained doesn’t quite fit the bill. The combat is stiff, the player classes are imbalanced, enemies can spawn out of thin air to ♥♥♥♥ you up, and there are only three planets you have to backtrack to for what passes for the main story. But once I came to grips with those shortcomings, I found the game oddly engrossing. It’s a creative setting, with cool guns to shoot and a challenge I can mostly work my way past. This is no Dark Souls killer, but Immortal: Unchained brings some new features to the mix along with some great level design and solid looting.

It's a souls-like with focus on guns. There is melee, but is clearly pushed aside so you can focus more on shooting enemies. Reloading adds to the challenge in combat.

+ Level design is great. Obelisks (checkpoints) are spread near enough to fill your ammo but far enough to make you save your healing.
+ Lore is everywhere (collectible) if you're into that.
+ World design is nice and varied with 3 main planets with varying levels, traps and enemies.
+ Voice acting is not bad though there are only a handful of talking NPCs.

- Weapons are currently still unbalanced with shotguns and sniper rifles being the strongest and [strike]SMGs and ARs lacking power[/strike]. (edit: [b]SMGs and ARs got buffed![/b])
- Almost (if not) all enemies in the game are humanoid, so critspots are the same for every enemy.
-Bosses are not as challenging by themselves since you can stagger them continuosly (edit: [b]some bosses had their stagger bars adjusted[/b]), they make the bosses (and the rest of the game) harder by adding traps and adds to fights.
- The melee animation is hot garbage, luckily you'd be shooting more.
- Female character animations and features don't differ much from males.

-+ The game still has some bugs and no NG+ though the devs are currently active in the game discussion page taking suggestions and bug reports. They are also working on NG+ by the end of the year.

Overall, the price might be a bit too high but give it a "shot" if you're into souls-likes and want to try a different take.

Dark Souls with guns is pretty fitting. 
Death, failure mechanics are pretty much the same, even leveling and upgrading work pretty much like in Dark Souls.
However the game feels vastly different while playing: it's hard to describe, but the focus on ranged/gunplay works amazingly well. Videos'n pictures don't do the gameplay justice, the game plays simply like a charm. Controls are very responsive, weapons and enemy-attacks are well telegraphed and have a decent amount of impact. 

The sci-fi-setting is also very well done. From the getgo you are thrown in a world which will call you back every time you stop playing. As bleak and bland the game looks in soem let's plays, the more mysterious it becomes when playing. 
The overall visual design nailed the grand scale sci-fi can offer perfectly. 
The plot and the very well voiced slew of characters do the rest to suck you into the game-world. 
You will also find lore-bits all over the world, beeing it weapon/item/gear describtions or an incredible number of enemy-lore-drops or hidden lore-pickups. Lore is pretty much everywhere. 
The art-style, world-building and character-design do the rest to make the athmosphere very unique.

Technical the game looks quite good, animations aswell as textures are quite alright and i had 0 issues on my rather dated system with everything put on "high" and 1080p (i5, 1060, 16GB Ram, Win10).

Negatives i found: 
a) the soundtrack is kinda underwhelming
b) soundmixing of voices is strange in some places
c) weapon-sounds could be changed...shotguns sound like sci-fi-air-conditioners for example
d) balancing...oh my lord this is all over the place:
ammo is in way to short supply
enemy encounteres range more often then not between laughable easy or getting overwhelmed by a legion, this needs work
difficulty comes more from the number of enemies sometimes thrown at you at once
e) armor upgrades are linear, which means you find shrines which give you set upgrades (from carrying more med-packs, the damage reduction)...which takes away some customization. it's not terrible, but i would've prefered a classical approach. 
f) game feels overpriced....should probably go for 2/3 of the current price (september 2018). 

all in all i can fully recommend this game for fans of the Souls-like-genre. The moment to moment gameplay is spot on fun, the world and plot are quite unique and interesting...and i cannot stress enough how great combat feels. However be prepared to get frustrated with the amount of enemies thrown at you once in a while.

This is a great game. Just don't buy it and expect Dark Souls 4. This is its own game with its own quirks that you need to learn and adapt to. Most of the people giving this game negative reviews only have about 2-3 hours in it. Granted I was already loving the game by the 3 hour mark, but I have found most of the common complaints with this game to be unfounded. Let's take a look at some of those:

1. It takes too long to reload and heal.
- There are skills to reduce your reload and heal time.

2. You run out of ammo too fast.
- If you legitimately run out of ammo too fast then you are either using too weak of a weapon, are missing a ton, or never finish people with melee. You can always upgrade your weapon to increase its ammo capacity, and even find armor upgrade shrines that will eventually increase your overall ammo capacity.

3. Melee sucks.
- Melee builds can apparently work, but only once you've gotten a good weapon for it and skilled towards it. You can't start off with melee. It's typically going to be used to finish off weak enemies so you can save some ammunition. It does have other uses, however. You can break deployed shields with it and it has a special function against bosses. If you stagger a boss normally, they will flail a little and recover fairly quickly. However, if you stagger a boss with a melee attack then you'll knock them over and leave them vulnerable longer.

4. X gun type is bad.
- Some are, unfortunately. Hopefully the devs will balance things like SMGs and assault rifles as they currently do too little damage. For the people complaining about snipers, though? Their aim just blows. Snipers can one shot even some big enemies and chunk bosses like crazy if you headshot them. Maybe don't start with them if you don't want to shuffle between your sniper and pistol (snipers have low ammo count because of their super high damage), but when you unlock a third weapon slot they are amazing. If you find yourself struggling to find a good weapon, the primary slot shotguns work very well.

5. Getting hit or rolling cancels your reload.
- Yeah it does. It's not bad design, it's made to force you away from the offensive for a time. Most enemies are melee in this game, and the ranged ones tend to be quick to kill. They need to balance out your firepower and force you to find a good window of opportunity to reload, especially in boss fights. If you think it takes too long to reload? Once again, there is a skill to reduce your reload times.

This really is a great game. The devs did very well and I hope more people actually give it a chance and try to learn the game rather than bash it for doing things differently from Dark Souls. The game looks great, locations are incredibly different from one another, gunplay works very well and its got some nuances to it that really surprised me. I can't really recommend this game enough.

to the game itself,  it's really fun and challenging with amazing boss fights. At the beginning, don't get fooled by the "Prologue" level at the start,  it looks all very similar and can turn people off,  but let me tell you that later level and enemy designs become much better and easier to maneuver around. 

each weapon class has it's own playstyle so it feels fresh if you wanna try another combination of guns and you gotta find out what combo you have to hit an enemy to bring him down fast and smooth. the trick is pretty much find the weakness like shoot arms or legs off and try to hit his weakspot , not all weakspot are in the back btw , some are in the front,  and with a good gun you don't need hit only weakspot to kill someone fast. 

the most important tip is to look around there are sooo many secret passage ways and hidden areas , and often shortcuts that you can go easily back to your obelisk to regain ammo and level up and so on,  I never felt unfair if you really open your eyes , the obelisks "bonfires" are much more fair then any dark soul games. 

the second most important tip is , find your favorite gun and upgrade it , you will see on higher levels they do so much nicer damage and you will feel really satisfied with how fast enemies die. 

another good thing is that you yes start with an "Class" which has it's own beginner stats and one passive bonus at start,  but  same as in soul games you aren't bound to stick to the same weapons as the class suggests you to use , for example if you start as marksman (sniper) you can still build out your character to play with shotguns effectively later on,  which I really love and appreciate, you aren't bound to one class like many other RPGs.

all in all its an awesome game with many souls like feelings and designs , but with it's own original charm,  I really recommend playing this game, I didn't wanna write an review but I feel it's so unfair and false to listen to those negative reviews,  many of which played maybe less then 2-3 hours,  don't listen to them , I would say if you unsure maybe watch some gameplay videos and then decide for yourself,  I had lots of fun and gonna play it more , hopefully with an new game plus mode,  and btw this game was made with an relatively small development group,  so cut them some slack,  they really did an amazing job with this game and I hope they bring out dlcs and an part 2.

[h1] In A Nutshell [/h1]

🔵 [b] Pros [/b]
+ Interesting, original sci-fi setting and lore.
+ Good variety of character development possibilities.
+ Good replay-ability with different builds.
+ Good variety of equipment types and enemies.
+ Decent optimization.

🔴 [b] Cons [/b]
- Major lack of polishing.
- Very poor enemy AI / pathfinding.
- Several boss fights are badly designed and/or lackluster.
- Numerous balance issues.
- Above average quantity of minor glitches and bugs.

Immortal Unchained can only be defined as a proper "mixed bag". On one side, we find an interesting setting, good loot, character building and upgeading systems, and also interesting maps and enemy variety. On the other though, we also find several major issues, a general noticeable lack of polish that really gives out a sense of "unfinished work", and some of the most ridiculous AI patterns seen in a good while. 

As in any Souls-Like game, expect a very hard challenge where death is commonplace, with enemies dishing out tremendous amounts of damage, insidious traps behind every corner, and tactical fast-paced combat where split-second dodging and timing are of the essence. One of the good points is the variety of class choices, spacing from long-range snipers, hybrid jack-of-all-trades, to specialized brutal warriors only using melee. This favors replay-ability, as restarting with a different build means an entirely different play-style and experience.

Overall, I found the experience to be pleasant despite all the various issues it might have: killing tough enemies and finding hidden loot around levels still gives out satisfaction, so the "regular" gameplay is quite good, tense, and difficult just like it should be. This cannot be said for boss fights, mostly as they are either lackluster, boring, or with major design flaws, and since this is a Souls-Like, bosses should be the exact opposite.

[h1] In-depth Feature Analysis [/h1]


🎮 [b] Gameplay [/b]
Immortal Unchained proposes pretty classical Souls-Like gameplay, featuring many mechanics in common with the legendary series. A central hub, called The Core, will be your base of operations, while portals leading to various worlds will be the access point to increasingly difficult levels. Once a world Commander is beaten, the next world can be unlocked. Each level is free-roaming and has several static checkpoints, or Obelisks, scattered around, acting as resurrection points in case of death, and safe areas. 

Of course, in each zone there are a lot of secret areas to discover, also many boxes, doors and bridges that can only be unlocked later, when enough key items have been acquired to do so. In Immortal's case, such items are called Decrees and Protocols, collected by looting or from special enemies, are fundamental to open all the hidden areas in each world. Loot is randomly assigned and can be dropped from both enemies and containers. Weapons acquired will often have attribute requirements to be used: this is where character building comes into play at Obelisks, players are able to pay an increasing fee of Bits to augment the character's attributes, to create a custom build.

Weapons can be upgraded with components, found from scrapping unused gear, or looted from enemies and containers, plus a fee in Bits. Each weapon has unique pre-installed attachments, granting special abilities: for example, a sniper rifle with a grenade launcher will be able to throw explosives as special attack, consuming Energy (mana) in the process, while an SMG with silencers or sights will be more accurate and less detectable. This is a very interesting part of the game, too bad many attachments and statistics are not described and you can only suppose what they do exactly.


📖 [b] Story [/b]
Story is composed of cut-scenes after certain events happen, and many bits of lore scattered around the various worlds, points of interest, and even NPCs that will tell you their stories, among other things. As in many games of this type, so much is left to interpretation, and details are purposefully scarce.


👊 [b] Combat System [/b]
Combat, as in any Souls-Like, is all about perfectly timed dodges, understanding enemy attack patterns, and attacking at the right moment. Some interesting mechanics are present, such as Stability: when hitting an enemy many times in sequence, especially at their legs, it will lose more and more stability, ultimately leading to it losing balance and being staggered for some time. Another good mechanic is the presence of weak points, such as heads and glowing parts in the enemy bodies, so accuracy and flanking are rewarded with much greater damage.

Armor penetration, weapon scaling percentages, and damage types such as energy, fire, acid and more, are all factors to consider in battle: some weapons and strategies working one moment could be useless against the next new enemy.

One of the biggest issues of combat mechanics is that some enemies, especially in close melee, have a tendency to perform "homing" attacks, rotating in unnatural and almost glitchy ways during animations, in order to get the right angle to hit you, and in many cases they succeed. I found dodging in this game to be quite unreliable compared to other similar titles.


💰 [b] Content & Pricing [/b]
Priced at a whopping 50€ default tag, even if pleasant for some features, this is not a title I recommend at this price. The game itself is more than sufficient, the price for the proposed quality instead, is not. As I said before, get it now only if you just need another souls-like in your life now, else really, wait for a sale and possibly a few patches. As stated by devs, the game lasts 20-30 hours depending on play style and skill.


🔗 [b] Balance & Challenge [/b]
Challenge, as expected, is very high and punishing, though some forgiving aspects also exists, such as chance to recover lost Bits if you fall down a ledge, in the point before you dropped down. Balancing has issues, clearly favoring Ranged over Melee approaches, as majority of enemies will be Melee, ranged even if limited by ammo, gives a great edge especially with DPS builds. 

Some boss fights are outright badly designed, featuring nonsense such as homing ranged undodgeable attacks, or additional mobs spawning at ridiculous rates all the time. One thing, the right one, is making the challenge tough but also fair, another is making the game unfair to create artificial challenge. In this, immortal Unchained disappointed me greatly.



[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]


🎥 [b] Graphics [/b]
Quite remarkable, powered by the modern Stingray Engine. Models are of good quality, while textures and environments are a bit inconsistent, depends where you go and where you look. There is a marked pop-in of shaders and vegetation as you walk, not proper popping but rather a slow fade-in, which is quite irritating.


🔊 [b] Sound [/b]
Average quality of sound effects and music.


🔩 [b] Performance & Stability [/b]
Game is optimized quite well, and there are no major issues. (GTX1080, i7 4820K, 16GB RAM)


💻 [b] Artificial Intelligence [/b]
Very poor. AI will often get stuck in objects or just not find the way to you, while other times, they will sense your presence from incredible distances and come from the other side of the map.


🏠 [b] Quality of Life [/b]
Decent enough, no issues to report.


🐛 [b] Bugs & Issues [/b]
Several minor bugs of graphical nature, and some problems with enemy charging animations on stairs.



[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
Immortal Unchained is a decent souls-like at the core, but with also many issues that combined hold it back from being truly a good game. It feels like a missed chance to make something really great.

To save you some effort - every single boss for the first three zones does *exactly* the same with some minor twists, and it simply ramps the damage up in various ways. Boss tries to keep you in front so it can demolish you, you try and get round the back so you can one shot it.

Sci-fi third person shooter Souls clone. Great idea, terrible execution filled with conflicting design.

The game wants you to:

Shoot enemies in the head but headshots don't do enough damage to make your ammunition last.
Shoot enemies in the their back but it's all narrow corridors and open areas are filled with traps and spawn triggers.
Shoot at close range but you can't reload while sprinting or dodging and your walk speed is too slow to dodge ANY attack.
Mix melee and gunplay but melee is a single 3 hit combo limited by stamina with no parry, block or counter system.
The game wants you to shoot enemies in the limbs to stagger them but this is a waste of ammo on most enemies.
Bait enemies into attacking to expose their weakpoints but most enemies have a punish or follow up attack.

There's little satisfaction or flow to the combat. Then partway through it's like they just gave up and you get constant enemies spawning right in front of you. The melee ones have a buildup and a chance to react but the range ones teleport in and shoot nigh instantly, this includes enemies with a hit scan laser that can two shot you.

Boss fights so far are actually good and prove that this idea can work, dancing around their moveset and unloading into their weakspot. Early maps are ok but later ones are a confusing labyrinth with no navigational aids at all.

This game is at least functional (I did have a single hard crash which lost me a fair chunk of progress) but I can't recommend it unless they give it a serious overhaul.

It's not like this is lacking in concept, and I actually believe more competent development could have made this work.

Unfortunately, this game just doesn't work, and that's all down to the lacking execution and some major mistakes in mechanics. And what developers trying to make their soulslike clones seem to ignore is that Dark Souls perseveres with its incredibly smooth and fluid style of play. As soon as that instantaneous and responsiveness goes away, you end up with trash like Lords of the Fallen and The Surge. And sadly, this is where I:U falls.

The gunplay as a whole is cumbersome and tacky, which is its main downfall. The aiming and responsiveness of the camera is really janky. But what's mainly jarring is this compromise between making it half over-the-shoulder shooter and half soulslike. The game should have never built itself around the ability (and benefits) of free aiming. It just doens't work combined with the nature of Soulslikes (dodging, stamina systems, flinching, etc). It honestly just feels like Souls' melee systen at a distance - you shoot, the enemy shoots, you dodge, you reload, you shoot. The fact you are using a gun at range feels almost inconsequential. Yet at the same time, this distance combat nullifies the nuance in Soulslike combat where you retreat or close the gaps with your enemies. Instead you try to cheese things by corner hugging, and it's just flat out boring.

An example of irritation is also enemy weakpoints. Most enemies have weakpoints you expose by maneuver (like their back). Great, huh? No, because dodging in this game is horrid. Enemies seem to auto turn even if they are in an animation. Also, you can't seem to quickstep while not in lock on, which is majorly horrible. The only way to realistically get around the back of enemies is to just run in free aim, but another major kicker to this is there is no quick way to snap the camera to where your character is facing, which is another massive oversight.

It also seems really bizarre how much HP mook enemies have. The flow of Dark Souls is often kept alive by the fact that enemies may be able to two shot you, but you also 2-3 shot them. Even the most disposable of enemies here take several ammo clips to dispatch. It's infuriating and utterly kills the flow, making repetitive lame strategies take precedent rather than a few good shots that don't require running around like an idiot trying to expose an enemy's back. Multiple enemy encounters also don't work. As soon as you meet two enemies in play, you may as well forget trying anything clever.

Also, **** whoever thought it was a great idea to not have invincible frames when you get knocked down. That's 2-3 seconds where anything can follow up KO you, and there's nothing you can do about it. I can almost understand a boss doing this, but being sent to the ground via a loose grenade to merely be killed by a stray bullet while my character is uncontrollable is inexcusable.

This needed more testing and going back to the drawing board. I can't believe beta testers didn't pick up on some of the nonsense found here.

wanted desperately to like this game. conceptually interesting: a mix between a shooter, Souls and dungeon-crawling with limited RPG aspects. 

unfortunately, it doesn't (or at least hasn't) translated well into play. in fairness, i've only played a little into the game (up to first boss), but what i've seen so far leaves a lot to be desired. 

first off, as a shooter, the controls feel sluggish and you do not actually get an intuitive feel for the shooting mechanic. a lot of that can be attributed to the terrible cross-hair design. for a game which boasts of gameplay mechanics which allow you to target critical points and shoot off limbs, it doesn't feel precise enough. even playing as a sniper/marksman with sniper rifle, it's not exactly clear where the aiming point/hit box is and should be. 

also, after a while, in a game where bullets are scarce, shooting off limbs is pretty much a waste of bullets because they regenerate in the course of combat! as a sniper, your ammo is very scarce indeed, and some enemies cannot be one shot-ed even if you headshot or weakpoint (back) shot them. so, after accidentally shooting off the arm off a gun-wielding grunt mob (thanks crosshair), i noticed that "hey no gun!", i might be able to use this tactic for hard-to-kill mobs with guns - i.e. i'd shoot off their hand wielding weapon and then switch to melee to finish them off thus saving precious bullets. ingenious. up the point when the gun and arm respawns 1 to 2 seconds in rendering that bullet useless anyway. waste, they could have made that a viable mechanic. but this is a good example of how much potential the game has, and yet doesn't use it properly or ♥♥♥♥♥ it up. 

the melee-element of the game is also very basic at least at this point and is limited to button-mashing and dodging. while being able to hack off limbs makes the game sound visceral and meaty, there's no oomph and weight to the melee combat which comes across as almost an after-thought. think melee combat in Counterstrike (except you're limited in stamina) and you won't be far off. zzz. actually, CS:GO melee might be a little bit more invigorating ... at least you don't run out of stamina after 5 seconds. 

the AI is both tepid and supernaturally-gifted at spotting you at the same time. pathing leave much to be desired. i've literally seen the AI-mob retracing it's path 10x in a semi-circle trying to walk to where i am (one block of debris in between us). 

the boss fight was pretty horrid. it seems to want to follow a Souls-type formula, with bosses hitting hard and following specific fight patterns which you learn to recognize. unfortunately, the sluggish combat and generally off shooting mechanism doesn't translate into anything remotely fun. the fight area is small also (which already kind of breaks the Souls rule that boss areas should generally be big so players can run around and have enough space and time to learn the boss mechanics). 

the level design is pretty bad at least for the first level. linear and narrow corridors. its hard to distinguish directions and turns and every other room looks the same. again maybe just the 1st level and the rest of the game may be better later on. also, combat spaces are very tight, which is fine for a melee-oriented close combat game but not for game where main damage output is shooting-based. 

the colour and art is bleak and drab. perhaps that is intentional, but it just lacks colour and life and makes everything damn dreary. that combined with the sluggish combat make it almost a chore to play the game. 

i'll give it another go. perhaps it's one of those games that gets better (i hope a lot better) as you progress. but right now, it says a lot for the game that less than 1 hour in and i do not feel like playing it anymore. if the 1st level is anything to go by, i do not have a lot of hope.

i'd say for now at least, the number of hours played is as good an indication of how bad i feel this game is for me. i have gone so far as to uninstall it, thinking that it's unlikely i'd ever want to come back to it. maybe someday.

Awesome new entry in the Soulsborne subgenre of hardcore RPGs. Couldn't have come at a better time too, since we have to wait until 2019 to play the next batch of AAA Soulsborne games. 

WARNING: This game is hardcore. I'm a Soulsborne veteran (beat all 3 dark souls games multiple times, 70+ hours in Nioh, played the crap out of the Surge, etc.), and I think Immortal Unchained is probably the hardest of them all. It throws lots of traps and powerful enemies at you, while giving you fewest healing items of all Soulsborne games and requiring above-average awareness. And yet, the enemies all telegraph their attacks very well and the mechanics are very clear and it's not fake difficulty. It's a real challenge!

PROS:
- guns & grenades work great and compliment the mechanics well
- new mechanics and unique setting make the game feel fresh and unique within the genre
- very atmospheric
- difficult as hell but also fair
- lots of enemy types
- lots of RPG customization
- huge levels with lots of places to explore
- complex sci-fi story

CONS:
- badly optimized (depending on area, game runs anywhere in the 20-60fps range on a PC that easily runs games like Battlefield 1, Dark Souls 3, and Far Cry 5 on extreme graphic settings at 50-60fps) 
- no wearable armor (only permanent buffs you unlock that count as armor) 
- no multiplayer

Some reviewers have commented that mechanics in this game don't work. Nothing could be further from the truth. Mechanics are genius. You have to worry about ammo (reloading takes time), positioning (enemies take a lot more damage if you hit them in the back), and aiming (when you can't hit an enemy in the back, you gotta be handy with the controller to get those headshots off from a distance). It's all very challenging and completely fresh genre-wise. 

If you're a Soulsborne fan, don't miss on this one.

Interesting idea but very poor execution, too many fundemental issues

PROS
- The theme of the game is kinda unique and the story is presented in a way that's easier to follow than Dark Souls.
- I think the weapon upgrade system was kinda cool and it's nice that you can break down useless weapons for upgrade parts
- The game feels somewhat challenging
- The music and audio was decent
- It's an interesting take on the souls like genre and I can appreciate them trying something different with this game

CONS
- This game has some of the worst, least intuative level design I've ever seen in a souls-like, This is one of the few games I've played where I felt the need to watch a walkthough video to see where I actually had to go.
- The combination of the artstyle, graphics and theme often leaves you disoriented, in some parts of the game everything looks the same, there's not enough detail in the world to make referance points in your head making navigation very difficult especially when combined with the poorly thought out level design
- For some classes the lack of ammo can be quite annoying early on
- The range in which you can actually shoot an enemy is quite short, If you stand roughly 20 metres away from a mob and shoot them with the Sniper rifle the bullet won't damage them
- Extremely poor AI, there's a sweet spot in which you can stand a certain distrance from an enemy and shoot them but they won't aggro you
- The transitions of the character movements such as dodging, shooting, melee and sprinting lack fluidity and at times feel quite abrupt
- Poor balance, don't pick the sniper class, you'll regret it very quickly due to very limited ammo and extremely long reload times.
- Reloading is infuriating in this game, you press reload and it takes about 3 seconds HOWEVER during that reload if you sprint or dodge you need to reload all over again even if you we're 99% finished reloading.
- The secondary charged attacks from your weapon are cancelled completely if you let go of the button a fraction too early which doesn't feel right, instead I think you should still be able to use your secondary fire without a full charge at the cost of less damage and resource usage
- The game has a AAA price tag when it by no means feels like a AAA game, the animations, fluidity and overall presentation feel very "Indie" In it's current state I feel the game is worth half it's current price tag
